name: Palauan
confidence_why: Carlson 1968 treats primary stress as phonemic at the word level (final or penultimate, no minimal pairs) and Josephs 1975, 1990 and 1997 mark stress on every multisyllabic word because 'in many cases it is impossible to predict' which syllable carries it, but Wilson 1972 argues that stress is regular penultimate once unpronounced underlying stem-final vowels are posited and that the claim of unpredictability 'is not true', and Josephs 1997 himself allows that a 'rather complicated' rule could probably be written for native words.
catalog_citation: Carlson, Clayton H. 1968. Palauan phonology. MA thesis (Linguistics), University of Hawaii. 86 pp. Ch. IV 'Suprasegmentals'. Open copy: UH ScholarSpace hdl 10125/35988.
catalog_locator: p. 59, section 'Stress'; Notes to Chapter IV, note 1, p. 62; cf. p. 17 and summary p. 61
catalog_quote: Palauan has three noticeable degrees of stress: weak (unmarked), secondary [`], and primary [´]. ... Only primary stress is considered phonemic on the word level since both weak and secondary stress can be predicted once primary stress has been ascertained. On non-compound words (base plus affixes) primary stress is found only on the final or penultimate syllable.¹ Examples of final stress are: /beáb/ 'rat' /ʔoʔóy/ 'yes' /melát/ 'to tear' /belúw/ 'village, country' /meŋdúb/ 'to swim' /meŋdeʔdúʔ/ 'to speak'. Examples of penultimate stress: /ktíkit/ 'a fish' /ʔádow/ 'roof' /ʔomróbr/ 'to snatch' /klálow/ 'thing'. There have been no minimal pairs found for primary stress. [Notes to Chapter IV, note 1, p. 62] Stress is predictably final in forms that have suffixed object or possessive pronouns.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each word has one primary stress, which is lexically specified (phonemic) but confined to a two-syllable window at the right edge: it falls on either the final or the penultimate syllable of a (non-compound) word, and its position cannot in general be predicted from the surface form (Josephs 1997:28 'in many cases it is impossible to predict which syllable.. will be the stressed one'; his dictionary marks stress on every entry). Morphology fixes it in part: possessor and object-pronoun suffixes always carry the stress (surface-final), prefixes never do, and unstressed vowels reduce to schwa or delete. Generative analyses (Wilson 1972:39; Flora 1974 apud Zuraw 2003) derive the surface final/penult split from regular penultimate stress on abstract underlying forms with final vowels that later delete, so that 'surface stress is normally on the final syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Carlson: weak and secondary stress are predictable from primary stress (secondary in free variation with weak on full vowels adjacent to the primary-stressed syllable). Wilson 1972:39: 'an irregular phenomenon of secondary stress which generally occurs two or three syllables before the penult', not analysed.
new_statements.exceptions: Grammatical words er, me, el, ke, te (and tȩ, ȩr) are always unstressed (Josephs 1975 n.6; 1997 Note 19); suffixed object/possessor pronouns always stressed (Carlson n.1; Josephs 1975 3.x, 6.x); zero 3pl object suffix leaves stress on the stem (Josephs 1975:176); compounds excluded from Carlson's window statement; Wilson: polysyllabic suffixes may be stressed, prefixes never.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (citation forms, 'non-compound words = base plus affixes'); Carlson separately treats phrase pitch levels 1-4 as predictable from primary stress. Wilson's penult rule applies to underlying representations after morpheme concatenation, not to surface syllables.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe standard Palauan (pala1344, ISO pau) as spoken in Koror/Babeldaob; Carlson 1968 notes minor dialect variation but his stress statement is language-wide. No sub-variety issue.

new_statements.quote: As we saw earlier in 1.3.2.b, in any Palauan multisyllabic word, only one syllable will be stressed, while all the others will be unstressed (e.g., me-nge-LE-bed, de-CHU-dech, chel-de-che-DUCH, etc.). The stressed syllable of a word can be quickly identified because it is pronounced more loudly and strongly than the nearby syllables. One-syllable words of Palauan (except for pronouns and other short words like er, el, etc.) are automatically stressed (e.g., MAD, BUCH, KALL, etc.). || (11) All Palauan possessor suffixes are stressed. (12) When a (stressed) possessor suffix is added to a Palauan noun stem, any originally stressed vowel in that noun stem becomes unstressed.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record has an empty rule; the existing statement (Carlson 1968: primary stress final or penultimate, unpredictable) and the already-read Handbook ch. 1 note 18 ('in many cases it is impossible to predict which syllable.. will be the stressed one') read lexical (unpredictable). The remaining chapters agree with that and add: culminative single stress, monosyllable/clitic behaviour, suffixes (possessor, object pronoun) always stressed, stem stress preserved under reduplication, loanword final-stress tendency, and the 24.3 remark that native-word rules 'could probably' be developed though complicated. All examples are compatible with Carlson's final-or-penult restriction. Differs from…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Exactly one stressed syllable per multisyllabic word (louder, stronger); content monosyllables are stressed, clitic monosyllables (pronouns, er, el) are not. No positional rule is given for stems; instead stress is morphologically attracted: possessor suffixes (3.3.1) and object-pronoun suffixes in perfective verbs (6.4.1.c, 6.8: 'the object pronoun suffixes.. are always stressed, leaving all the other syllables in the word unstressed') always carry the stress, the zero 3pl-nonhuman suffix cannot attract it, and reduplication keeps the stem's stressed syllable (11.1.1: 'the very same syllable that is stressed in the original word maintains its stress in the reduplicated form'). Vol. 2 sec. 24.3, p. 354: 'Although our analysis would turn out to be rather complicated, we could probably develop a set of rules to predict which syllable will get stressed in any native Palauan (multisyllabic) word. When we observe the occurrence of stress in loanwords, however, we cannot find any consistent patterns to predict the position of the stressed syllable, except perhaps that there is a tendency for stress to be placed on the word-final syllable.' Every cited example falls on the final or penultimate syllable (re-KAS, me-che-RO-cher, me-CHED, e-LO-lem, BA-dre, me-SIL, se-ba-DONG, tochelbeteRIR).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None recognized: 'only one syllable will be stressed, while all the others will be unstressed' (vol. 1 p. 98); unstressed syllables show vowel weakening to weak E.
new_statements.exceptions: Clitic monosyllables (pronouns, er, el) unstressed; zero suffix (3pl nonhuman object) has no phonetic content and cannot attract stress, so the stem syllable stays stressed (to-CHOLB, KUIMD, vol. 1 pp. 243-244); some unstressed syllables keep full E (number words e-LO-lem, reduplicated CE- syllables, possessed te-MEL); loanwords: stress shifts freely from the source position with a tendency to final stress (Sp. sabado > se-ba-DONG, calabozo > ke-le-BUS, trompeta > trom-be-TANG, vol. 2 pp. 354-355); Eng. sign > saing noted as 'an unusual stress pattern -- namely, sa-ING' (vol. 2 p. 367, image page-384). Vol. 2 (chs. 13-24) is syntax and has no phonology chapter; the Teacher's Manuals reproduce the same chapter list.
new_statements.identity_note: The Handbook describes standard Palauan as taught in Palau public schools (Koror, Ministry of Education); vol. 2 ch. 24 discusses stress in loanwords from Spanish, German, Japanese and English specifically, not native vocabulary.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction on placement. Josephs' Handbook (1997) treats Palauan as having one stressed syllable per word with no positional rule for stems and morphological attraction to possessor and object-pronoun suffixes; every cited example lands on the final or penultimate syllable, matching Carlson 1968's 'final or penultimate' restriction. Two minor tensions: (a) Josephs recognizes no secondary stress ('all the others will be unstressed'), whereas Carlson posits predictable weak and secondary stress; (b) within Josephs, ch. 1 note 18 says stress position is 'in many cases impossible to predict' while vol. 2 sec. 24.3 says a 'rather complicated' set of rules 'could probably' be developed for native words -- both still deny any simple positional rule, and 24.3 adds that loanwords show no consistent pattern except a tendency to word-final stress. Finer 1987 could not be opened.

sources.citation: Josephs, Lewis S. 1975. Palauan Reference Grammar. Honolulu: University Press of Hawaii (OA reissue, ScholarSpace hdl 10125/62896).
sources.note: Sec. 1.4.2 (pp.20-21 of OA PDF): every word of two or more syllables has just one stressed syllable, louder and stronger; stress marked with an accent in transcriptions; schwa only in unstressed syllables; possessor and object-pronoun suffixes always stressed (3.x, 6.x). No positional rule is given; stress is treated as a marked lexical property ('the stress falls on one of the syllables of the verb stem', p.176).

sources.citation: Wilson, Helen Irene. 1972. The phonology and syntax of Palauan verb affixes. PhD dissertation, University of Hawaii (= UH Working Papers in Linguistics 4(5)).
sources.note: Sec. 3.2 pp.39-40: 'Primary stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel in a word of two or more syllables.. Stress is assigned once all the syntactic rules have combined the morphemes.. suffixes of more than one syllable may be stressed although prefixes are never stressed. There is an irregular phenomenon of secondary stress which generally occurs two or three syllables before the penult.. Surface stress is normally on the final syllable because of the later rules which reduce and/or delete the unstressed ultimate vowel.' Also p.(ch.2): criticises Dyen for treating stress as unpredictable.

sources.citation: Zuraw, Kie. 2003. Vowel reduction in Palauan reduplicants. In Proceedings of AFLA 8 (MIT Working Papers in Linguistics 44), 385-398.
sources.note: Unstressed vowels reduce; several suffixes attract stress, de-stressing the stem vowel (following Flora 1974's underlying-final-vowel analysis); most stems mono- or disyllabic 'usually with initial stress'; reduplicants unstressed. No general positional rule stated.

sources.citation: Conant, Carlos Everett. 1915. Notes on the phonology of the Palau language. Journal of the American Oriental Society 35: 1-15.
sources.note: Historical-comparative only: unaccented vowels indistinct/eroded, Indonesian final vowels lost if unaccented in Palau, accented vowels retained; no synchronic rule for where the accent falls.

sources.citation: Finer, Daniel L. (1987). Reduplication And Verbal Morphology In Palauan. The Linguistic Review 6. Walter de Gruyter. pp. 99-130.
sources.note: No placement statement to set against the catalog's lexical coding (Carlson 1968: phonemic primary stress on the final or penultimate syllable). What the paper shows incidentally is compatible with the record: the stress marks on the free forms in (24)-(25) fall on the final or penultimate syllable and vary lexically (sáik vs blekéu, uréor vs klakoád), and the stressed possessor suffix -(ŋ)ék overriding stem stress matches the on-file Josephs 1997 Handbook statement that possessor suffixes are always stressed and Zuraw 2003's 'suffixes attract stress'. Nothing contradicts the catalog.
